title: 对谈 Modal 联合创始人 Erik Bernhardsson：AI 智能体该用什么样的沙箱
author: LangChain
content:
Brief Description

Modal co-founder Erik Bernhardsson explains how the company built its inference, training, and sandbox infrastructure and where he thinks AI workloads are headed.

Table of Contents

  • What Modal builds for inference, training, and sandboxes
  • Was Modal built for AI workloads before ChatGPT?
  • What made Modal's sandboxes finally take off?
  • Why Modal is moving sandboxes from gVisor to VMs
  • Should the agent harness run inside the sandbox?
  • Do agents need a full VM or a lightweight sandbox?
  • Are open source models close enough to swap in?
  • When is RL worth it over supervised fine-tuning?
  • Why Modal built auto and shared inference endpoints
  • Can reinforcement learning be packaged as a product?
  • What Modal is building next for training and batch jobs
  • Why Modal built a team of forward deployed engineers
  • How Modal uses coding agents and MCP servers internally
  • Why Erik is bullish on voice to voice models

What Modal builds for inference, training, and sandboxes

Host: Thank you for being here, Erik. Excited to have you here.

Guest: Yeah, it's awesome to be here.

Host: Modal has been one of my favorite companies to watch grow up. You guys do a lot of stuff now. Would you maybe, could you talk a little bit about all the things you do and how you think they fit together?

Guest: Yeah, so Modal, for you who have not tried us out, we build AI infrastructure, roughly, is how I would put it. We power a lot of customers like Cognition, Decagon, Suno, Runway, a lot of inference, a lot of training, a lot of sandboxes. It's a fairly general purpose platform. You can use it for pretty wide range of stuff, though. But we've obviously seen, with all the Gen AI stuff, a lot of demand for, in particular, inference, like LLM, audio, video inference, but also sandboxes. It's been kind of more recently, in the last 12 months, something that's been exploding.

Was Modal built for AI workloads before ChatGPT?

Host: And you guys started before ChatGPT, right? Like, when was the company founded?

Guest: Little bit before. So we started a company early 2021 and then kind of struggled a little bit to figure out what we're doing. It's funny, actually. We started just a few blocks from here. But then ChatGPT came in late 2022. Stable Diffusion also came actually right after, and Stable Diffusion in particular ended up being like a killer app for us in the first year or two.

Host: Did you know that, like, when you were building Modal, this, again, like 2021, year or two before ChatGPT, did you know enough about, like, what the AI workloads would look like, so that you were building for that, or were you just building generic kind of infrastructure that was really easy to adapt to that as it became clear what it would look like?

Guest: I mean, we're the latter, actually. Like, I think one of the benefits of building an infrastructure, I mean, we're like very deep in the infra layer. We think a lot about file systems and container runtimes and scheduling and that kind of stuff. And I always thought, like, one of the benefits of being in that layer is, like, you don't necessarily have to move, like, super fast with every trend. You have to take a little bit more of a longer term perspective and think about the building blocks and the primitives. We launched a serverless function product in 2021. It took actually one or two years to see product-market fit, and then we launched a sandbox product in 2023, and we didn't see that growing until 2025. So I always thought of, like, infrastructure is like a little bit more, like, slightly more longer term.

You kind of build the right primitives and the right building blocks, and then we're obviously very lucky with all this Gen AI stuff. That's been tremendous for us. We're quite well positioned. AI was something we thought about, but we always thought of Modal as, like, AI, data, machine learning, compute-intensive stuff, HPC, and then Gen AI just came and it just, like, pulled us so hard in that direction.

What made Modal's sandboxes finally take off?

Host: Let's talk about sandboxes for a little bit, maybe. I think you tweeted at some point that was your fastest growing product. What happened to make it take off?

Guest: There's a bunch of stuff. So sandboxes, again, we launched it actually back in 2023, and the observation back then was basically something like, it's like me and Akshat, my co-founder, kind of talking over lunch one day, and we're like, there's all these people using LLMs to generate code. Well, clearly they need a place to run that code, and we realized we actually had almost all the infrastructure to do that really well. So we launched that product. Like I mentioned, it didn't really take off until two years later. What started happening back in about a year ago, it's like customers started initially doing a lot of vibe coding. So companies like Lovable, or many other ones, were starting to basically, like, build apps from prompts, and they needed a place to execute that code. So that was, like, the first use case.

After that, a lot of people started using Modal for background agents. So we have some customers like Ramp. They run the Ramp Inspect on Modal, which is basically their own internal background agent for coding. And then the third major use case that's actually been crazy large for us has been reinforcement learning. Not, like, a massive amount of customers, but the customers that use us run at, like, absurd scale. So we're talking about some millions of sandboxes, constant rollouts, and a lot of the reinforcement learning models, especially for coding, they need a way to execute that. So we've powered reinforcement learning for Meta and some other customers.

Host: And when you think about these three different use cases, the coding agent, the background agent, reinforcement learning, are the sandbox primitives the same across all of them, or are there differences in terms of what's...

Guest: Fairly similar. I mean, at a core, like, you need a programmatic way to, like, create a container from an image, run code in it, interact with it from the outside without, obviously, the agent sort of escaping the sandbox, which I've seen some news about that. So the interface is, like, pretty simple, that there's some more advanced stuff, like there's some cool stuff around, like, snapshotting sandboxes, code, cloning sandboxes. We're working on stuff like that. But I think to me the differentiation in the space has primarily been around, can you do that at very large scale? Can you do that with good performance? Can you do that reliably? We're like infra geeks. So for us, like, those are just things we're, like, very good at. And I think that explains why in the sandbox space, we've seen really strong adoption, and very solid.

I don't know the market share number, but I imagine we're by far the biggest vendor in the sandbox space. I think that's been more the sort of the differentiation. And from the outside, it's like, going back to your point, it's fairly similar access has been this, like, kind of nice fundamental building block for a lot of these applications.

Why Modal is moving sandboxes from gVisor to VMs

Host: Yeah. Another thing I'm curious about is it seems like pretty similar to a lot of the stuff you guys were doing even before that, in terms of just, like, spinning things up really quickly and provisioning.

Guest: Totally.

Host: So, like, how much, like, sandbox-specific stuff did you have to build on top of the underlying primitives that you guys already had?

Guest: Not a whole lot to release the first version. Akshat, our CTO and co-founder, he built the first version of sandboxes in like two days, and then we kind of, like, put it out there, and not a lot happened for two years. But once we started seeing some growth, like, we had to rearchitect some of the internal systems just to handle, like, very, very large rollouts and scale. So we've had to rebuild some of that, like the core infrastructure. But a lot of the foundational stuff, like I mentioned, we built our file system, for instance, like, that file system powering sandboxes is very good for very fast loading of, or cold starts of, containers. We've had to go in to look at running full virtual machines more recently. So that's a very sandbox-specific thing. We previously used a runtime called gVisor.

We're switching a lot to virtual machines right now. And...

Host: Why, out of curiosity?

Guest: It's primarily because some customers want to run, like, more full operating systems. So gVisor has some limitations, but with, in particular, running Docker, but also, I mean, with a full VM you can do stuff like mess around with, I don't know, firewall rules or whatever. Like, you can do anything inside these sandboxes, really, plus a little bit of a performance improvement. So we're also looking at actually, like, running, like, Windows sandboxes and stuff like that, maybe Mac too. Like, there's some interesting stuff there.

Should the agent harness run inside the sandbox?

Host: Interesting. One perception I had, at least at the start, was that there were maybe, like, different types of sandboxes. There was ones that were, like, really, you'd send, like, maybe really quick to spin up but weren't super stateful. So you'd send, like, just simple kind of, like, code you want to evaluate, and then there's more, like, stateful ones for long-running agents. Is that, like, a true distinction? Are they actually the same? How do you think about that, and what you guys want to be good at?

Guest: I think that's roughly right. I will say, though, like, we've seen a lot of people wanting long-lived sort of stateful sandboxes. My view, this is a little bit of a hot take, is that a lot of that just reflects like kind of poor architectural choices from, like, the harnesses. Like, we have this, like, kind of dominant architecture where, like, the harness often runs, like, with the code itself inside the sandbox, and so naturally people want to run that for, like, 24 hours inside a sandbox. I think the future of agent harnesses is actually a decoupling where, like, you have a harness that's running for a very long time, but the sandboxes are more ephemeral, maybe one for every tool call, even. I do think our median sandbox life cycle is something like 12 seconds, but we have a very long tail of, like, 24 hours and stuff like that.

But, yeah, I'm more of a, long term, I think a lot of sandboxes will generally be very short-lived.

Host: I feel like this, like, Anthropic wrote their blog post separating, kind of, like, the hands from the brain. And I'd say, like, before that, when I was talking to people who are building agents, like, it was maybe 50/50 whether they'd run it in the sandbox or do it separate. Now I feel like it's maybe, like, 75 or 80% running it outside and connecting. Is that, like, the trend you're seeing as well? It sounds like you think that's where it should go.

Guest: I think that's where it should go, 'cause then you can do some really cool stuff, like, your kind of harness just, like, spin off, like, multiple subagents, like, cloning things, like, explore kind of a whole branch, like, bring it back, like, and snapshot things and kind of resume, like, restore things. So I think that's ultimately, like, where it kind of has to go, just architecturally. It's harder to build these things, and I think, I mean, it's, like, crazy, right? Like, software engineering has, like, changed, like, so fundamentally. I mean, I think you write a lot of code still, right? Like, I try to write a lot of code still. It's, like, so different in the last 6 months, 12 months, and so my view is, like, AI is here. It's, like, changed a lot of the types of software we can build, but it's obviously also changed, like, how we build software.

I kind of feel like a lot of the infrastructure and the tooling is still not quite, has, like, caught up with all of that. So I think we're going to see a lot of churn in, like, architectures and infrastructure. I mean, like, I think a lot about that with Modal because we're an infrastructure company, but I also think it applies to the agents and the harnesses and, maybe, companies like you. There's just going to be so many changes in the next 12 months, 24 months. Like, it's like when the mobile came, we had to come up with Objective-C, and then when internet came, we had to come up with Kubernetes and all these things. Like, I think it's the same thing with all these agent stuff. Like, we're going to have to come up with completely new infrastructure and completely new frameworks and all this stuff.

So I'm very excited about that.

Do agents need a full VM or a lightweight sandbox?

Host: Maybe one last question on sandboxes. There's this idea of kind of, like, lightweight pseudo-sandboxes. So, like, Pydantic Monty or just-bash from Vercel or QuickJS, where they're, like, a subset of the runtime, where a lot of the premise is you don't need a full sandbox. It kind of mocks it out. Do you have any thoughts on that and the usefulness or place for that?

Guest: I mean, maybe. Like, I think they could be useful for some stuff. Like, my general feeling is, like, a lot of the agents, like, today, like, they like to have, like, a fat, like, Linux box. Like, if anything, we've seen the pull in the opposite direction. We're moving from gVisor, which is, like, has, like, most of the surface area of a Linux, but we're moving away from it to virtual machines because there's like certain things that don't quite work in gVisor, and gVisor is, like, way more full-featured than a lot of these, like, if you go to, like, Wasm or V8 isolates or some of the stuff you mentioned. I don't know. Like, I think for certain use cases, when you want to run, like, an insane amount of, like, maybe they're good for, like, you take a small JavaScript snippet from a customer and you need to run it, like, a million times.

I think something like Wasm or V8 isolates or something like you mentioned could actually make sense. But I think for the general case, like, my feeling is, like, you kind of want these, like, big fat VMs.

Host: And does that also help with, like, computer use and things like that? Like, is that a driving force for these?

Guest: Totally. Yeah. And I don't think we're seeing it quite yet. But, like, one thought I'm very excited about is, in general, the big labs have obviously seen tremendous success with coding models because coding is, like, quite verifiable. You can do the rollouts. You can run things and see, and do post-training very efficiently on coding sandboxes. I think, as we're moving into, like, and you may have whatever thesis you want about this, but, like, automating white collar work more broadly, like, we're probably going to see a lot of people doing rollouts in, like, Windows and Mac sandboxes because, if you want to automate, like, computer use, or browsers for that matter, like, you kind of need to train agents that kind of, like, click around in Excel and then Outlook and Slack and Teams and Zoom, maybe even, I don't know.

Like, and so I'm kind of excited about that too over the next few years. So, I'm sure we're going to see a lot of demand for those things.

Are open source models close enough to swap in?

Host: Maybe taking that and going into kind of, like, inference, because you guys also play there.

Guest: Yeah.

Host: Yeah. How has your strategy for inference evolved over time?

Guest: Yeah. I mean, we support all the open source models. Pretty easy to deploy open source models on Modal. We also launched a couple of features around making it even easier. So we have a thing called auto endpoints, which is basically you can, like, point, like, one-click deploy a single-tenant Kimi K3 or something like that. We also have shared endpoints now, which is, like, more resource efficient because they're shared across a lot of users, just kind of off-the-shelf K3 models, etc. So we see a ton of demand. I think the sort of the conversation has shifted a lot in the last 12 months. I would say, like, a year ago, open source models were just not, nowhere, they were nowhere near the frontier models, right? And so the argument was more like, you can save a lot of money, like, you can fine-tune, like, and if you fine-tune or post-train, they're almost as good as, on specific use cases, they're almost as good as the frontier ones.

Now the, like, at least in the last three months, the open source models have been, like, basically as good as the frontier models. Well, now OpenAI and Anthropic just launched a bunch of new models. So, like, not, I think they pulled ahead again, but I think what's shifted the conversation a little bit has been you actually don't need as much post-training, maybe. So, like, we still see a lot of people post-training, but I think also a lot of people are just very happy to just, like, swap out Anthropic for Kimi K3 or DeepSeek 4.1 or something like that, and save basically two-thirds of the token cost, and the model is, like, basically as...

Host: How much of the inference going through you guys do you think is on, like, these custom fine-tuned, post-trained models versus just off-the-shelf Kimi K3, if you had to guesstimate?

Guest: I actually don't know. I would assume it's 50/50 at this point. But it's like 50/50 by volume. It's probably, like, by number of customers, I'm sure it's like 95% of customers just use off-the-shelf open source models, and then you have a 5% of... You always have this, like, skew. Same with, like, reinforcement learning. It's like a very small amount of customers who drive insane amount of usage. Most customers do not need to do post-training and stuff like that. I think...

Host: How do you think about that, like, 5% versus the skew, as like a founder and product leader? Like, are you building for the 5%? Do you want to do the long tail?

Guest: We're primarily building for sophisticated customers. Like, we've always considered Modal sort of a high-code tool. Like, we love engineers. Like, we never try to, like, we always wanted, like, Modal to be as powerful, if not more powerful, than existing tools, while getting rid of all the junk that previously sort of challenged people working with the cloud. I think, so to us, like, our core users are machine learning engineers, like researchers, like people building very sophisticated infrastructure or applications. I should say, we also have a long tail of, like, hobbyists, early stage startups. But I think it's important, like, we love also the power users, the people building very sophisticated stuff.

Host: Yeah, I think you guys have a great kind of, like, onboarding and very user-friendly console as well. So I think that absolutely appeals to the long tail as well.

When is RL worth it over supervised fine-tuning?

Host: For kind of, like, post-training, like supervised fine-tuning versus RL, like, what are you seeing people doing now? Has that changed over time?

Guest: We definitely, by number of users again, we see, like, way more just supervised fine-tuning, SFT, than reinforcement learning, but the very large customers, like the very complex customers, are doing reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning is a mess, though. Like, it's like you can get, like, better result than SFT, but it comes at a very high cost today. It's very sort of use case specific. You have to think about the rollouts. You have to think about, I mean, the infrastructure itself is, like, very tricky. You have to think about the evals, like the judges. It's very complex. So I don't think, I wouldn't suggest to anyone to do RL unless you really want to squeeze out those, like, x% of extra accuracy. But for some of our customers, like, that's worth it, right? Like, we have customers like Cognition, for instance.

Like, they run, like, very large-scale coding models, and for them, like, reinforcement learning is very much the right thing to do. I think for the average customer, fine-tuning is enough, or just running, frankly, just, like, off-the-shelf models and just having better prompts.

Why Modal built auto and shared inference endpoints

Host: For just, like, inference, you guys have gone from kind of, like, really low-level primitives to auto endpoints, and now it sounds like there's shared endpoints, which I just learned about now. Like, how do you think about, like, I'd say that's like going up the stack a little bit.

Guest: A little bit. Yeah.

Host: Yeah. How do you think about that? How do you make that decision? Yeah.

Guest: Yeah. I mean, we spent the first three, four years of the company building like very foundational stuff, like compute, runtime, file systems, like, stuff like that. I think over time, like, we're always going to go up the stack to some extent, when we see opportunities and we see a lot of demand for things. Like, we are in the infra layer very clearly, but I think with inference, for a long time, like, people would come to us and deploy LLM inference themselves. And these were relatively sophisticated customers, and they want to deploy things like vLLM or SGLang, and we would help them with that. But I would say, like, it's pretty hard to, like, tweak the performance of SGLang and vLLM. There's so many parameters and things like that. So I think it made a lot of sense for us to build shared endpoints and auto endpoints and make that process a little bit easier.

We're spending a lot of time on sort of, basically, self-optimizing performance. And the idea is, like, if you spin up an endpoint on Modal with some of these open source models, the performance gets better automatically over time, because we can sort of monitor the system and train draft models and tweak the batch sizes and all these things. There's so many different parameters. So some of that stuff, I think, makes a lot of sense for us to turn into product and package and sell that to a lot of customers.

Can reinforcement learning be packaged as a product?

Host: Do you think you'll do that for fine-tuning or RL? Like, you talk about how complicated it is and how it's hard to do RL, right? And is that something you try to make easier?

Guest: I think so. I think the dream is, over time, like, you want to turn these things and, like, package them up into products. I would say with fine-tuning, you see that a little bit. I think Tinker by Thinking Machines is an example of a product, is actually, it's pretty exciting. Like, they've actually been able to package it. It's relatively complex to use still, but it does take away a lot of the infrastructure challenges of doing SFT. I would love to figure out what that looks like for reinforcement learning. There's a lot of companies obviously thinking about this. Today, like, reinforcement learning is quite labor intensive. Like, it's very service heavy, but the dream is, like, can you package it up into, like, here's the thing, here's an RL in a box. I would love to figure that out.

I don't think we're quite yet there. Continual learning is, like, another thing that would be even better to do. Maybe give it a year. Like, I'm sure there's going to be stuff on the market. We're thinking a lot about it.

What Modal is building next for training and batch jobs

Host: You mentioned that early on you built a lot of these foundational things that you're now packaging up a little bit more. Are there, like, current foundational things that you guys are working on?

Guest: Working on a training product. I'm pretty excited about that. So you've always been able to train a model on single node, but we're building a product for multi-node training. So basically the idea is, like, you can spin up, like, sort of a serverless cluster of 4, 8, 16 nodes, so, like, 128 GPUs or something like that, fully interconnected with RDMA. So that's a product. We have a number of design partners. We're very excited. We're going to launch that hopefully in next few weeks, actually. We're working on a batch product. So the idea is, like, we have often periods of excess capacity, and we also have customers who have things that are very latency insensitive. Maybe, we had a customer the other day that was, they were transcribing 5,000 years of audio. So they had millions and millions of audio files, and they just wanted to transcribe all of those audio files, and it's like one of those things, you got to just chug through that, like, very long list of audio files, and you can sort of do that during periods of, like, it takes like multiple, it took, like, a couple weeks.

So we're launching a product where you can queue up sort of background jobs, and we'll kind of, like, go through that queue, and we'll give users a big discount. So, up to 50% discount for background tasks, which is kind of exciting.

Why Modal built a team of forward deployed engineers

Host: And I want to finish by maybe talking about, like, Modal the company a bit. Like, you're building an incredible company. We have a lot of startup founders here as well. Maybe a few questions there, starting with, like, you come from an infra background. And I think you describe Modal as kind of, like, an infrastructure company at its core when it started. As you move, like, up the stack and you start to do things that are maybe, like you mentioned, RL, very services heavy, the people doing those services are probably different than infrastructure folks. Is that changing kind of, like, the DNA of the company? Are you guys evolving in some way there?

Guest: Yeah, I think that's right. I mean, we built up, like, a very large team of FDEs, forward deployed engineers. I think we had, like, three at the beginning of this year, and now we have 25. And so, and the truth is, like, building AI applications is pretty hard. Like, so we think it's very important to build up team of really solid engineers that can work in a more customer engaged, like, basically sit with customers and help them build model, or, like, build really cool things and optimize things.

Host: Can you maybe, like, double-click on that? Because I think FDE is, like, the hottest job thing. Like, what does it mean at Modal to be an FDE?

Guest: Yeah. And by the way, I think it was Palantir that came up originally with the name, and there's an argument that, like, maybe everyone is, like, kind of not doing it the way Palantir do it, because Palantir was, like, you would fly someone to Brazil for, like, three months. We don't quite do that. But we have people go to, like, a customer and sit with them for a few days at a time, maybe, and so it's about, it's about fixing bugs, like helping them optimize models, like sometimes helping them build things or helping them architect things, helping them look at their code and see if you can structure it more efficiently. I mean, we're entering a new world of building applications in a fundamentally different way. I think in the long run, all software will, to some extent, be AI native, like, we won't talk, it's like software that's, like, internet native, like, or it's kind of a, you don't talk about it that way.

Like, I think in certain ways, like, all software will become AI native in a certain way. So you need people to help customers with that. I'm sure you've experienced the same thing. Do you have...

Host: 30, 40, probably more than that? We have a big deployed engineering team.

How Modal uses coding agents and MCP servers internally

Guest: Yeah.

Host: What you mentioned, kind of, like, coding and how that's changing, like, how do you think that's changed for you, but also as a company, like, how do you try to make your own company more AI native in terms of coding and software development?

Guest: I mean, pretty much every engineer at Modal uses AI all the time, including myself, for writing code. It's obviously complete game changer for writing code. I mean, is it, like, a 10x change? I don't know, but it's, like, a 2x, 3x change is kind of what I feel like. I use it a lot myself. It's like an intern you can sort of delegate the boring tasks to. Sometimes you can delegate very complex tasks too. Interestingly, we've actually seen that the more experienced, the older engineers, like, are actually using it more, because I kind of feel like they're actually, like, maybe it's, like, kind of like thinking about as interns. Like, if you're, like, a new engineer, maybe it's, like, harder to delegate things. Whereas, like, if you have, like, 20 years of experience and suddenly someone gives you 20 interns, you can, like, yeah, you do that, you do that.

Like, so we've seen, like, some of our, like, more experienced people who, like, use agents, like, crazy, like, writing hundreds of thousands of lines overnight for some prototype or something. So that's been pretty cool to see.

Host: And what does the harness for doing that look like? Like, are you guys using cloud agents a bunch? Do you have some, like, in-house harness that people are running locally? Like, how...

Guest: No, we, I mean, we let people pick and choose. So initially was all Cursor. Now, more recently, it's been Claude and Codex, and some people are playing around with open source things like Nightshift and, with all the OpenCode, and all of those things. We don't mandate anything. I think our view is that this space is moving so fast. We kind of want people to, we want a little bit of, like, internal competition. We thought about building our own harness internally, just as more of, like, a kind of a dogfooding, because we think long-term Modal is a great platform for hosting harnesses. So, we thought about, maybe we should build our own harness to learn what it feels like to host a harness on Modal. We'll see.

Host: Do you dogfood some of, like, the inference stuff as well? Have you guys trained a model of your own?

Guest: No. We probably should, though. That's a good idea. Yeah.

Host: You've got more than enough other things to do.

Guest: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But actually a lot of people use our own Kimi K3 deployments for, like, Claude and things like that.

Host: Awesome. How are you seeing kind of, like, AI transform other areas of the business besides software engineering? Like, we talk about coding a bunch. Are you seeing the same in sales or go-to-market or people or other functions you guys have?

Guest: I think so. I mean, I've been using chat and Claude pretty efficiently. Like, we have internal MCP servers that hook up to our CRM and our revenue data and all these things. And it's kind of cool. You can go into, like, the other day I was, like, I was going to London for a few days. So, I just, like, kind of tried it out. I'm like, ask Claude, like, what are some customers I should reach out to, and it's like, scan all the CRM and everything. It's like, here's, like, a list of customers. And so, and I know the sales team does a lot of that. So, I'm sure you see the same thing. There's some really cool stuff, I think, in go-to-market that you can do using these agents. I don't know about, like, other, like, HR and legal. I would, I feel like they're a little bit behind, but eventually I'm sure we get there too.

Why Erik is bullish on voice to voice models

Host: Maybe last question I have for you. You have an incredible kind of, like, view into the industry and vantage point. What is something that, like, you're most excited about that you think is really about to kind of, like, take off?

Guest: Like, kind of a random thing, I've always been very bullish on is, like, voice models. Like, I feel like they're, like, not quite there yet, but, like, once you can really talk to a computer the way you talk to a human, my feeling is like that's going to be a game changer for, like, how we interact with computer systems. Not maybe for everything, but I feel like, so, like, and in terms of, like, what that means for infrastructure, we're very excited about, like, low latency inference for that reason, and, like, streaming media, like audio and video. So that's, like, one thing that I'm very excited about.

Host: And does this mean kind of, like, voice to voice, the native multimodal stuff?

Guest: Exactly. Voice to voice, right? Like, and it's like when you talk to a computer using voice to voice today, like, it still doesn't have the same fidelity and the latency. It doesn't feel like a human. It's, like, very uncanny. But, like, I give it, like, six months, give it 12 months. I have a feeling the models will be very good.

Host: All right, we'll keep an eye out for that. Well, thank you, Erik, for joining us. Thanks for all the wisdom.

Guest: Thank you.
aiSummary: Modal 联合创始人解释了 AI 基础设施为何既需要低成本沙箱，也需要完整的虚拟机。
oneSentenceSummary: Modal 联合创始人解释了 AI 基础设施为何既需要低成本沙箱，也需要完整的虚拟机。
summary: Modal 联合创始人 Erik Bernhardsson 回顾了沙箱需求的三波增长。最早是通过提示词生成应用的用户需要运行代码，随后是后台编码智能体，接着是要大规模运行轨迹的强化学习团队。他解释了 Modal 为何将部分负载从 gVisor 迁到完整的虚拟机，也提出一种架构思路：让智能体的控制程序长时间运行，按需创建和销毁短寿命沙箱。他还谈到共享推理端点能省掉哪些调优工作、为什么多数客户用不上强化学习，以及如何利用空闲算力降低后台批处理的成本。

mainPoints.point: 三类负载先后带动沙箱需求
mainPoints.explanation: 通过提示词生成的应用最早需要执行环境，其后是后台智能体，最后是需要运行大量轨迹的强化学习用户。

mainPoints.point: 把智能体控制程序与执行环境分开
mainPoints.explanation: Bernhardsson 预计，长期运行的控制程序会按需创建短寿命沙箱。他估计 Modal 沙箱的生命周期中位数约为 12 秒，长尾可达 24 小时。
完整虚拟机在运行 Docker 和配置防火墙等方面更灵活。需要反复执行的小代码片段仍可能适合 Wasm 或 V8 隔离环境。

mainPoints.point: 推理运维比强化学习更容易产品化
mainPoints.explanation: Modal 可以通过调整批次大小、训练草稿模型来优化端点性能。强化学习仍需要昂贵的轨迹采样、针对具体任务的评估和相应的基础设施。

mainPoints.point: 用空闲算力处理可以等待的任务
mainPoints.explanation: 有客户要转录总时长据称达 5000 年的音频档案。Modal 希望用价格更低的后台任务来承接这类负载。

keyQuotes: 我们的沙箱生命周期中位数大约是 12 秒，但长尾也有持续 24 小时的。
不过，强化学习这事相当复杂。
像 Wasm 或 V8 隔离环境这类方案，在某些场景确实说得通。
